# Similar Agendas, Diverse Strategies: The Quest for a Regional Hub of Higher Education in Hong Kong and Singapore
David Chan^(1) and Pak Tee Ng^(2)
1 Department of Asian & International Studies, City University of Hong Kong, 83 Tat Chee Avenue, Kowloon Tong, Kowloon, Hong Kong.
E-mail: chan.david@cityu.edu.hk.
National Institute of Education, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.
E-mail: paktee.ng@nie.edu.sg.
This article examines the approaches that Hong Kong and Singapore are taking to develop themselves as 'regional hubs of higher education' and the implications of their approaches. It starts with a delineation of how the internationalization of higher education structurally alters the landscape of the global higher education market. These changes drive both Hong Kong and Singapore to compete for the higher education pie. Despite many similarities in the vision and policy instruments, the article argues that there are significant differences in terms of their implementation approaches. More importantly, such differences reflect the different mindsets of the two governments in their governance of the university sector. Higher Education Policy (2008) 21, 487–503. doi:10.1057/hep.2008.19
Keywords: regional hub; internationalization; transnational education; Hong Kong; Singapore
## The Internationalization of Higher Education in East Asia
For a long time, academia in East Asia was a shielded and isolated industry.^(1) Prestigious universities were satisfied with their predominant positions from either a local or a regional perspective. The lack of world-wide competition allowed higher education institutions to enjoy an elitist atmosphere in a sheltered world (Postiglione, 2007; Yonezawa, 2007). However, globalization has broken down national borders and has blurred many differences among societies (Ohmae, 1990; Urry, 1998). This has led to a systemization of world knowledge, upon which ideas, people and resources have been fused in different ways (Denman, 2000). In response to this global trend, many higher education institutions now need to establish linkages with the international academic community, as part of the strategy to develop themselves as 'worldclass universities'. Moreover, they need to achieve or surpass international benchmarks in teaching and research. That is why global league tables are now
taken as a powerful indicator to prove and advertise the standard of universities in the marketized global education market. These ranking exercises are taken seriously by many governments and universities in East Asia and the influences of such indicators are growing rapidly in the academic field (Mok, 2007).
Climbing up the international university league tables is seen as an important step towards the internationalization of higher education. However, as pointed out by Knight and de Wit (1995, 15), internationalization of higher education is 'the process of integrating an international dimension into the teaching, research and service functions of an institution of higher education', with the international dimension to be introduced into higher education as 'a perspective, activity or programme which introduces or integrates an international/ intercultural/global outlook into the major functions of a university or college'. According to Knight (2006, 18), the internationalization of higher education involves both campus-based activities and cross-border initiatives with a wide diversity of activities, including 'international cooperation and development projects; institutional agreements and networks; the international/intercultural dimension of the teaching/learning process, curriculum and research; campusbased extracurricular clubs and activities; mobility of academics through exchange, field work, sabbaticals and consultancy work; recruitment of international students; student exchange programs and semesters abroad; joint/double degree programs; twinning partnerships; and branch campuses'. Therefore, internationalization should not be limited to only climbing up league tables. It should be targeted at building an international platform for the higher education sector.
This article addresses two aspects of internationalization of higher education. The first is that of increasing student mobility world-wide. Conventionally, students move from developing countries, where the higher education sector usually cannot meet the demands for tertiary education in the society, to developed countries, such as the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, where the education systems are more advanced. More and more students are doing so nowadays. Many students in East Asia, including those from our present case studies of Hong Kong and Singapore, still continue to seek tertiary education in the above English-speaking countries. However, different East Asian countries, for example Hong Kong and Singapore, are now attempting to draw international students to come to their higher education institutions, and there is an increasing number of such students. Therefore, there is increased student mobility as higher education internationalizes.
The second aspect of the internationalization of higher education in East Asia is that of the increasing erosion of boundaries among different higher educational systems world-wide. This is reflected by the rapid growth of
transnational or cross-border higher education, which is 'the movement of people, knowledge, programs, providers and curriculum across national or regional jurisdictional borders' (Knight, 2006, 18). Though cross-border education initiatives 'can be an element in development cooperation projects, academic exchange programs and commercial initiatives', in many cases, they 'are commercial in nature and are usually intended to be for profit'. These activities can be understood as a movement along the 'continuum from face-toface (taking various forms from students traveling abroad and campuses abroad) to distance learning (using a range of technologies and including e-learning)'. Cross-border education is a modality in the continuum (Knight, 2006, 19). The emergence of cross-border education is fuelled by the inclusion of higher education as an industry under the framework of the General Agreement on Trade in Service (GATS) (Knight, 2002). As a consequence, many countries in the region, such as Hong Kong and Singapore, have actively opened their education markets to foreign education providers for them to establish off-shore campuses, implement twinning programmes and so on.
In general, higher education sectors in East Asia are facing much more pressure and competition from their counterparts in the global marketplace. Hence, different higher education stakeholders, including governments, higher education institutions, student bodies, quality assurance and accreditation bodies, academic recognition bodies and professional bodies, are expected to respond these changes proactively and strategically (UNESCO, 2005).
This paper aims to examine how two cities in East Asia, Hong Kong and Singapore try to develop themselves as the 'regional hub of higher education', in the light of higher education internationalization. It examines the recent higher education reforms in Hong Kong and the parallel developments in Singapore and compares the similarities and differences in terms of their policy motivation and implementation approaches, thereby contrasting the meaning of 'regional hub of higher education', as it is used by the two governments.
## Strategies for Developing Hong Kong as a Regional Higher Education Hub
### Policy background
Hong Kong's higher education basically completed its massification of higher education in the early 1990s, and thus moved on towards the pursuit of quality and excellence after the mid-1990s (Cheng, 2001). The Hong Kong government and its educational authorities (e.g. the University Grants Committee) have put great efforts in reforming the higher education sector by adopting the principles of managerialism, which stresses the efficiency and cost-effectiveness in the late 1990s. By the turn of the new century, the Hong Kong government
began to bring in new elements to its higher education reforms, with managerialism still continuing to play a key role in driving the higher education sector. In 2000, the Hong Kong government published the Review of Education System Reform Proposal, which urged the government to provide educational opportunities for its people to develop their global competencies and skills in order to sustain Hong Kong's competitiveness in the knowledgebased economy (Education Commission, 2000). In response to the proposal, the then Chief Executive decided to expand the higher education sector by doubling sub-degree places by the year 2010 (Tung, 2000). In addition, in the 2004 Policy Address, he further indicated the ambition of promoting Hong Kong as 'Asia's world city, on par with the role that New York plays in North America and London in Europe' (Tung, 2004, cited in UGC, 2004a: 5).
The University Grants Committee (UGC), the executive arm of the government in planning and implementing higher education policies, further linked this vision and ambition with its policies of role differentiation and deep collaboration for the local universities, claiming that in steering the degreeawarding sector, and in assuring the local higher education institutions to follow their assigned roles and missions, laid the key to promoting Hong Kong's higher education (UGC, 2004a, b). Indeed, we could trace the UGC's perspective of this vision to an earlier time. Its Review Report in 2002 has already pointed out that:
The ambition to be Asia's world city is a worthy one, but there is no doubt that realization of that vision is only possible if it is based upon the platform of a very strong education and higher education sector. There are very good reasons for that which have to do with what universities are and what makes them excellent. (UGC, 2002, 1)
This ambition was further echoed by the then Chief of the Education and Manpower Bureau by proposing to develop Hong Kong to become the 'regional hub of education'. With this in mind, the Hong Kong government set up a special committee chaired by the then Chief Secretary to develop plans to engage Hong Kong in the international trade on higher education services for the region (Li, 2006). It is against such a policy background that new policies and regulatory frameworks slowly evolve. The following sections briefly describe and comment on those policies which aim to achieve this vision.
### The policies
The UGC-funded institutions played a dominant role in the degree-awarding sector in Hong Kong. Private institutions only constituted a very small proportion of the higher education provisions. Although the situation has not
fundamentally changed, the recent reforms have indicated the government's further commitment of involving private institutions in higher education provision. The upgrading and renaming of Shue Yan University led this 35-year-old institution becoming the first private university in Hong Kong. More importantly, this marked a break in the monopoly of degree-awarding status held by publicly funded universities or programmes that were run in association with other overseas universities.
In addition, the government has set the target of getting 60% of secondary school leavers into tertiary education by the year 2010. This forges another round of massification of higher education. 'In achieving this target, the government will facilitate the task for tertiary institutions, private enterprises and other organizations of providing options other than the traditional sixth form education, such as professional diploma courses and sub-degree courses' (Tung, 2000, 23). In response to the government's call for further massification of higher education, the Education Commission (EC) proposes three major components in its Review of Education System Proposal for the provisions of tertiary education, namely: (a) universities, that is, degree-awarding educational institutions; (b) post-secondary colleges, that is, institutions that offer courses above secondary level, usually for high-school graduates; and (c) continuing education institutions, that is, education institutions that provide different types of courses and programmes above secondary level, usually for people who are working in the day-time (EC, 2000).
The proposal indicates that privatization, as an efficient way to diversify the higher education system so as to allow students more choices, will be a possible trend with the expected rapid growth of associate degree programmes by community colleges that are not funded by the government (Lo and Tai, 2003). In fact, in recent years, numerous community colleges have been established to provide sub-degree programmes, including associate degrees, higher diplomas, professional diplomas and other post-secondary programmes of equivalent standard on a self-financing basis. Currently, there are 20 such institutions that are offering full-time accredited self-financing sub-degree programmes, and all the UGC-funded institutions have joined in this new market by establishing their own community colleges or continuing education units, which can be seen as 'semi-private' institutions in themselves. Although these sub-degree programmes are operated on a self-financing basis, the government provides a package of financial assistance schemes to eligible students, including meanstested grants, low-interest loans, non-means-tested loans and travel subsidies (EMB, 2006). This demonstrates that, in the process of privatizing higher education, the Hong Kong government has adopted a 'public-aided approach' to transform the higher education landscape from a public dominance mode to a public–private mix mode.
The continuing education units of the UGC-funded institutions are also actively engaged in developing distance-learning courses, conversion courses and other continuing education programmes in collaboration with other overseas universities. Unlike Singapore and Malaysia, where the government directly intervenes in shaping the development of joint programmes, the Hong Kong government has adopted a far more liberal approach in allowing the market forces to decide upon the higher education market. Foreign universities can easily enter into the Hong Kong market. But to maintain basic quality control, all courses conducted in Hong Kong leading to the award of non-local higher academic qualifications (including sub-degree, degree, postgraduate or other post-secondary levels of qualifications), or professional qualifications, must be either properly registered or exempted from registration.
Any overseas institution is required to obtain accreditation, or other formal permission, from the Education Bureau (EDB) prior to its operation. This category is diverse, ranging from compulsory registration to formal assessment of academic criteria. The EDB will normally seek the independent expert advice of the Hong Kong Council for Accreditation of Academic and Vocational Qualifications (HKCAAVQ) as to whether a course or programme meets the necessary criteria for either registration or exemption from registration. However, the relevant requirements are considered to be straightforward and non-burdensome. It is noted that the Hong Kong government tends not to directly curb and regulate the quality, content, level and cost of courses and programmes offered by foreign educational institutions. Instead, the government heavily relies on the market mechanism for adjustments, where the government's main role is to provide sufficient information for consumers to make a choice (Yang, 2006).
Based on the above principles, the government regulations mainly focus on working as a gate-keeper on quality assurance in order to protect the consumers. According to Section 10 of the Non-local Higher and Professional Education (Regulation) Ordinance Cap 493, the Registrar of Non-local Higher and Professional Education Courses will approve the registration of a course if it meets the criteria listed below:
- (a) In the case of a course leading to the award of non-local higher academic qualification by a non-local institution, the institution must be a recognized non-local institution; effective measures must be in place to ensure that the standard of the course offered is maintained at a level comparable to a course leading to the same qualification conducted in its home country; and this comparability in standard must be recognized by the institution, the academic community and the relevant accreditation authority (if any) of the home country.
- (b) As for a course leading to the award of non-local professional qualification by a non-local professional body, the professional body must itself recognize the course for the purpose of awarding the qualification or for the purpose of preparing students for the sitting of the relevant professional examinations; and the professional body must also be generally recognized in its home country as an authoritative and representative professional body in the relevant profession. - (c) Satisfactory arrangements for payment and refund of the fee charged for the course. All the fees as well as the arrangements for payment and refund of fees and charges approved by the Registrar should be stated clearly in the contract with students (quoted in EDB, 2008).
It is noteworthy that the above registration requirement does not apply to the programmes conducted in collaboration with the specified local higher education institutions. If these local institutions certify that the course meets the criteria required for registration, in terms of both the standing of the institution/professional body and the quality assurance and recognition status of the courses, these jointly conducted courses/programmes will be exempted from registration. These institutions include: City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong Shue Yan University, Lingnan University, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Polytechnic University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Open University of Hong Kong and the University of Hong Kong (EDB, 2008).
The moderately liberal regulatory approach to transnational higher education has started to attract overseas education institutions in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia to compete for this newly emerging higher education market by providing courses in forms of joint programmes, distance-learning as well as twinning programmes. Transnational education in Hong Kong is only provided in the form of external, joint or distance programmes. Up to now, there is no branch campus of a foreign university in Hong Kong. This is probably because the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) Government works rather differently from the Singaporean and Malaysian governments, which invited foreign universities to set up their branch campuses in their territories. However, in view of the China market, overseas institutions have become increasingly proactive in setting up their academic programmes in Hong Kong in the last few years to attract mainland students (Yang, 2006). As of December 2007, the number of non-local higher education programmes in Hong Kong was 1,173, among which 426 (36%) were registered, while 747 (64%) were exempted courses. Regarding the source countries of course providers, most institutions were from developed
English-speaking countries, with the United Kingdom, Australia and the United States being the most popular exporters of education to Hong Kong (EDB, 2008).
It is worth noting that mainland China is also expanding its market share since top universities from mainland China have also offered their programmes in Hong Kong. Since Hong Kong and mainland China have signed a memorandum on mutual recognition of academic degrees in higher education in 2004, degree programmes offered by universities in mainland China no longer need to be registered in Hong Kong. Hence, the new policy framework attracts more and more Chinese universities to operate courses and programmes in the HKSAR. For example, Tsinghua University and Beijing University, in collaboration with HKU SPACE and Hong Kong Shue Yan University, offer academic programmes ranging from professional certificates to master's degrees in law, economy, literature and architecture, respectively. Most recent figures show that the market share of exempted courses by Chinese universities has stood at 9% in 2005 and 2006, and that of registered courses has grown from 5% in 2005 to 6% in 2006. Such an increase reflects the closer relations and interactions between Hong Kong and the mainland.
The rapid expansion of sub-degree and continuing education programmes has diversified the provisions of higher education in Hong Kong. As a consequence, an education market has slowly emerged and is becoming more mature in the higher education sector. Universities are now required to compete with each other and, therefore, tend to reform their curricula design in accordance to the market needs. Vocational-oriented studies have become popular subjects in local universities. To increase their competitiveness, some universities have started to revise their programme structures and to provide more opportunities in terms of international student exchange programmes, internship programmes, double major programmes and so on, in order to attract more talented students.
All these changes are a form of marketization, which represents a move from the traditional teacher-oriented paradigm to a learner-oriented one (Mok, 2005). In addition, they provide many more choices in terms of courses, and thus attract more students with different needs and expectations to come to Hong Kong.
## Parallel Developments in Singapore
### Policy background
Similar to Hong Kong's vision, Singapore aims to become the 'Boston of Asia' or 'a Mecca for diplomas, degrees and higher education' (Duhamel, 2004, 40).
Responding to globalization and the advent of the knowledge economy, the Singapore government attempts to reform its entire education system to enhance its competitiveness in the global marketplace. The official vision, Thinking Schools, Learning Nation (TSLN), implemented in 1997, is a key strategy for Singapore to achieve this aim. This vision has guided Singapore's educational development ever since (Ng, 2007). It is a vision for a total learning environment, including students, teachers, parents, workers, companies, community organizations and the government. Thinking Schools is a vision of a school system that can develop creative thinking skills, lifelong learning passion and nationalistic commitment in the young. Learning Nation is a vision of learning as a national culture, where creativity and innovation flourish at every level of society (Ng, 2005a, b). Generally speaking, under the TSLN vision, the government has introduced greater flexibility and autonomy in the education sector in order to maximize the students' potential and develop them to think independently and innovatively (Fitzpatrick, 2003). 'We hope to better develop each of our students to his full potential, so that he will be ready to face the challenges of the New Economy', said Teo Chee Hean, who was then Minister for Education (cited in Tan and Ng, 2007, 164).
In the higher education sector, the TSLN vision is interpreted and implemented as a move to enhance the publicly funded universities' autonomy and accountability. More autonomy in fiscal management and personnel matters is granted to allow the universities to find their own competitive edge. Meanwhile, through restructuring schemes and the introduction of quality audit and control, the government ensures that the universities will continue to fulfill their critical role of training graduate manpower for Singapore's economy (Ng and Tan, forthcoming). The University Corporatization Act in 2005, which is the embodiment of the twin strategies, changed the publicly funded universities into 'companies', while the government retains its control over the higher education sector through its national policy framework of higher education (Lee and Gopinathan, 2007).
Similar to the Hong Kong government, the Singapore government adopts 'autonomy' (diversification) and 'accountability' (government steering) as ways to reform the higher education sector in its pursuit of an 'education hub' status in the region. However, Singapore differs from Hong Kong in that it does not intend to expand its higher education sector too rapidly through a total freemarket mechanism, opting instead for a more controlled development in attracting new higher education providers, in the corporatizing of the existing universities, and in differentiating their educational goods and services. This difference fundamentally distinguishes the two cities from each other, despite their same ambitions of wanting to become a 'regional hub of higher education'.
### The policies
In order to develop the city-state as a 'regional hub of higher education', the Singapore government has strategically been inviting 'World Class Universities' (WCU) from abroad to set up operations in the country since the mid-1990s. These top universities in the world are invited by the government to set up Centres of Excellence in Singapore to spearhead research and development (R&D), transfer knowledge to the industry and position Singapore as an 'education hub' (MTI, 2002).
Today, various WCUs have set up centres in Singapore, including INSEAD (Institut Europe´en d'Administration des Affaires), University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Chicago Graduate School of Business, Georgia Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, Technische Universiteit Eindhoven and Technische Universita¨t Mu¨nchen. The government also encourages 'universities and institutes tie-ups' to put Singapore on the world map. For example, the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy of the National University of Singapore (NUS) has tied up with Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs (SIPA), London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) and the Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Paris to offer a double master's degree (Chia, 2007). The Singapore National Institute of Education (NIE) also launched a joint dual-degree educational doctorate with the Institute of Education, University of London in 2007.
The influx of foreign institutions to Singapore's higher education scene has added diversity to the educational goods and services offered, and the Singapore government has continued its effort to woo reputable foreign higher education players to come forth and play a part in it. However, there was a recent setback to such efforts. The University of New South Wales (UNSW) was set to develop its Asian campus in Singapore as the UNSW Asia, which was intended to be a comprehensive research and teaching university wholly owned by its parent institution, in providing a wide range of programmes from undergraduate to postgraduate levels. Its target was to recruit international students from across the region, while around 30% of its student population would be local Singaporeans (UNSW Singapore, 2007). UNSW Asia started its first student intake in March 2007. However, just barely two months into its operation, it suddenly announced its closure and complete pullout from Singapore, which was a great shock to both its staff and students. According to Professor Hilmer, the new UNSW Vice-chancellor, its sudden withdrawal was due to lower than anticipated enrolments and thus an unsustainable financial position would occur, which had the potential to pull the university down in the sense of soaking up all their uncommitted free reserves of A$200 million (S$255 million) (quoted in Davie, 2007).
There were other speculations in the media about the reasons and dynamics leading to the closure of UNSW Asia (see Ng and Tan, forthcoming, for a more detailed analysis). But, definitely, this is a setback to the Singapore government in its quest to become a 'regional hub of higher education'. However, all is not lost. In January 2008, Australia's Murdoch University, which has been offering subjects through the Singapore Manufacturing Federation's (SMa) School of Management, announced that it would be opening an International Study Centre within the SMa School of Management and would be making more subjects available to the market. According to Murdoch, the UNSW Asia's sudden pullout from Singapore did not affect its decision to increase its presence in Singapore, although it would be operating on a different model as compared to that of UNSW Asia (Cheney, 2008).
Therefore, despite some setbacks in the process, the development of transnational education in Singapore continues to internationalize Singapore's higher education, and helps Singapore to pursue a 'world-class' status in education. This also brings diversity in the higher education arena, giving local and international students more choices and reasons to pursue higher education in Singapore.
## Comparing the Strategies Adopted by Hong Kong and Singapore
Both Hong Kong and Singapore have adopted a diversification approach in order to develop themselves to be a 'regional hub of higher education'. Yet, there are differences in their implementation of the strategies. In Hong Kong, transnational education is taken as a sort of supplement to the local higher education sector, under the tide of the massification of higher education, where there is a free market in this sector. Basically, any institutions may enter the Hong Kong market if they want to. The government hardly rejects or supports any of these foreign higher education providers. The government simply relies on the market mechanisms to operate on this sector. But with such a laissezfaire approach both the quantity and quality of institutions and programmes can be rather diverse (Huang, 2006; Chan and Lo, 2007). In short, the Hong Kong government regards transnational higher education only as a supplementary sector and the motivation for allowing such a sector is simply for profit. Hence, one can say that this approach is quite neo-liberalist in nature.
In Singapore, allowing foreign universities to establish business in the country is a strategic move to build 'world-class universities'. Hence, the foreign education providers that can enter the market are usually top-notch universities in the world and have been specifically invited by the Singapore government (Lee and Gopinathan, 2007). Therefore, the number of institutions
entering the Singapore higher education market is limited and controlled. Only those regarded as renowned universities are invited to set up their business in the city-state. The government is generous with financial help to set up campuses in Singapore, but in return the universities are expected to live up to the government's expectations and to perform well. The closure of the Division of Biomedical Sciences of John Hopkins University in 2006 is such an example to demonstrate the strong position taken by the government (Lee and Gopinathan, 2007, 128). This shows that the introduction of transnational education in Singapore is a strategic move to enhance its higher education sector to achieve 'world-class' status. Therefore, the initiatives for diversification are controlled and measured.
## Discussion: What Does the 'Regional Hub of Higher Education' Mean to Hong Kong and Singapore?
Universities now operate in a highly competitive environment in the international higher education market, in which staff, students as well as competitors can come from anywhere in the world. In East Asia, competition is keen and pressure is high. But, the disappearance of boundaries between higher education systems also provides a chance to change the global educational landscape from a 'centre-periphery' pattern to a 'multi-centres' one (Altbach, 2002; Chan and Lo, 2008). This is the impetus for the quest for 'world-class' university in many countries and economies, such as China, Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong and Singapore. Every city wants to promote itself as a 'regional hub of higher education' or a variant of the same theme. However, we argue that the vision carries a different meaning for Hong Kong and Singapore.
In the case of Hong Kong, the government manages the higher education sector by splitting it into two parts. The first part is the conventional sector, which is mainly responsible for undergraduate, postgraduate and research programmes. The other part is the emerging sector, which mainly offers sub-degree programmes and continuing education. The Hong Kong government takes the former part as 'the core' of its higher education and retains a strong steering role in it, and regards the latter part as a 'supplementary sector' and is more liberal towards it. We suggest that this is a 'selectiveintervening approach' in university governance. The government proactively steers the development of the 'core part' by encouraging mergers between institutions, while leaving the 'supplementary part' loosely governed to encourage diversity in the market. With this approach, different stakeholders in the higher education sector will attach different meanings to it being a 'regional hub'.
With respect to the government, being a 'regional hub of higher education' means primarily an increase in the population of international students. Recently, the Hong Kong Chief Executive Donald Tsang decided to expand the population of international students by 'increasing the admission quotas for non-local students to local tertiary institutions, relaxing employment restrictions on non-local students, as well as providing scholarships' (Tsang, 2007, 40). Yet, for those few chosen universities (the University of Hong Kong, the Chinese University of Hong Kong and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), being a 'regional hub' under the differentiation policy means that they will have to climb up further in the international league table in order to attract more international students. For some of the other teaching institutions (e.g. the City University of Hong Kong), they need to strengthen their student recruitments in mainland China.^(2) Meanwhile, numerous existing and new institutions actively participate in the transnational education market which has been growing rapidly in response to both international and local calls for the diversification of funding and provision. These diverse developments reflect Hong Kong's 'selective-intervening approach' in the contexts of neo-liberal socio-economic circumstances. However, with a strong will to uphold (bureaucratic) accountability on the part of the government, such an approach does not really mean total institutional autonomy, and may result in tensions between individual institutions and the government. The recent Hong Kong Institute of Education's inquiry^(3) is a case reflecting such a tension.
In Singapore, education has been a supporting vehicle for the economy and therefore closely monitored and regulated. So, even though a higher education 'hub' implies global connectivity and diversity, what the Singapore government hopes to develop is still a managed and regulated 'hub', with a little more autonomy than before. In fact, many educational institutions in Singapore have been operating in a paradox of simultaneous centralization and decentralization (Ng, 2007; Tan and Ng, 2007; Ng, 2008; Ng and Tan, forthcoming). On the one hand, since the launch of the TSLN vision, universities in Singapore have been given more autonomy to reform their institutions to compete with the best in the world. On the other hand, the government's control over the sector has not been undermined. Indeed, 'autonomy' establishes a more 'decentred site' of governance in allowing the government to govern at a distance (Jayasuriya, 2005, 24). This is a 'thoroughly-regulating approach', one in which autonomy, innovation and diversity are confined within certain specified spaces and regulated by certain specified parameters. Therefore, the vision of being a 'regional hub of higher education' merely projects the country's ambition to achieve 'world-class' status regionally. The government is prepared to facilitate any development aligned with its intention but is always cautious at the governance level.
## Concluding Remarks
UNESCO recently published the Guidelines for Quality Provision in Crossborder Education, which recommended governments to:
- establish, or encourage the establishment of, a comprehensive, fair and transparent system of registration or licensing for cross-border higher education providers wishing to operate in their territory; - establish, or encourage the establishment of, a comprehensive capacity for reliable quality assurance and accreditation of cross-border higher education provision, recognizing that quality assurance and accreditation of crossborder higher education provision involves both sending and receiving countries; - consult and coordinate among the various competent bodies for quality assurance and accreditation both nationally and internationally; - provide accurate, reliable and easily accessible information on the criteria and standards for registration, licensure, quality assurance and accreditation of cross-border higher education, their consequences on the funding of students, institutions or programmes, where applicable, and their voluntary or mandatory nature (UNESCO, 2005, 13–14).
Comparing with the above recommendations, Singapore appears to have done more than Hong Kong in progressing towards a 'regional hub of higher education'. The Hong Kong approach is a neo-liberal one, especially in terms of licensing for cross-border higher education providers to operate in the city. Hong Kong relies heavily on the market to regulate itself, although the government has made a strategic attempt to strengthen its control over the 'core' part of the university sector. In contrast, the Singapore government's approach is more deliberate and measured. Licensing foreign higher education providers is not a random affair. Renowned foreign universities are carefully targeted and brought into the city-state.
From the comparative study of these two cities, two insights can be derived on the internationalization of higher education in various parts of the world. Firstly, despite the similar visions, we argue that different countries and cities will use different strategies based on their different socio-economic circumstances. Hong Kong's neo-liberal approach, which stands in great contrast with Singapore's regulated and measured approach, is a reflection of the fundamental differences in the political and cultural backdrops of the two cities. Secondly, we argue that the internationalization of higher education does not necessarily imply higher levels of academic freedom. In fact, the reverse may be true. The internationalization of higher education becomes an economic battlefield in which nations and cities plot to get ahead of their competitors. With the rise of managerialism (Burke, 2005) in the higher
education sector, accountability, economy, efficiency and effectiveness become key discourses in the academic circle across the globe. This provides a strong rationale for governments to take one intervention or another to shape the higher education arena. In the case of Hong Kong and Singapore, owing to the traditional Asian culture of compliance with the authorities, most government interventions do not cause serious conflicts between governments and higher education institutions (Petersen and Currie, 2008; Chan and Lo, 2008).
Nevertheless, with the influx of foreign higher education institutions with different academic traditions and cultural backgrounds, the political and cultural backdrop may change, and thus the responses to government interventions may be different in the future. In this regard, the future development of the higher education sectors in both Hong Kong and Singapore will remain worthy of our attention.

It also was alleged that Mrs. Law pressured the institute to fire four academics who publicly criticized the government's education policies, and that Professor Li told HKIEd vice-president Professor Bernard Luk, 'I'll remember this; you will pay' when Professor Luk refused to issue a statement condemning redundant teachers who went on strike in 2004. The report made by the commission of inquiry on the allegations concluded that Mrs. Law had improperly interfered with academic freedom, whereas the commission has found the allegation against Professor Li not established.
